question:
Patient note:
A 49-year-old woman is evaluated this morning in the regional block area prior to a scheduled elective right total knee replacement that the orthopaedic team anticipates will take approximately two hours under neuraxial anesthesia with a pneumatic tourniquet and primary cemented components; the plan is for immediate post-operative transfer to the joint-replacement ward and initiation of physical-therapy protocols tomorrow. She arrives on a stretcher, propped on pillows with the head of the bed elevated, and notes that progressive tricompartmental osteoarthritic pain over the past year has forced her to abandon her job as a catering supervisor and, more recently, to remain almost continuously recumbent because each attempt at weight bearing produces sharp medial knee grinding. Nursing flow sheets from the surgical admission that began yesterday document fewer than three assisted transfers to the bedside commode in a 24-hour period, and she states that at home during the preceding week she “basically lived between the mattress and the couch,” relying on her partner for meals, laundry, and bathing assistance. Her recent medical course is notable for having undergone a laparoscopic total hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy 22 days ago for symptomatic leiomyomata; the operation was uncomplicated, but convalescence overlapped with a longstanding ankle problem, and two weeks ago the podiatry service performed an endoscopic debridement and Broström ligament reconstruction of the left ankle to address chronic instability. At the conclusion of that latter procedure a molded fiberglass below-knee cylinder was applied and remains in place today, extending from just below the fibular head to the metatarsal heads with the ankle in neutral; she has been instructed to keep the cast non-weight-bearing until her first post-operative clinic visit next week, and therefore propels herself with a knee scooter only for short indoor distances. She emphatically denies sustaining any fracture at the time of the ankle operation, and radiographs in the chart confirm intact bony architecture; the intervention was entirely soft-tissue. Over the past month she has not experienced fever, chills, night sweats, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-lobe infiltrates, or any emergency evaluations for systemic infection, and the hysterectomy recovery was free of wound erythema or foul drainage. She has never carried a diagnosis of heart failure, emphysema, coronary disease, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, or clotting disorder, and she recounts no episodes of unilateral calf swelling, sudden dyspnea, or hemoptysis. No central venous catheter, PICC line, or implantable port has ever been placed; today’s only access is an 18-gauge peripheral IV in the right antecubital fossa. Maternal relatives have prominent leg veins, and she herself displays diffuse serpiginous bluish tributaries coursing along the posteromedial aspect of both calves that become more apparent when her feet dangle off the stretcher, though the skin is warm, supple, and free of pitting or focal tenderness. She denies prior heparin reactions, and outpatient laboratory data never showed platelet suppression. Medications this morning include acetaminophen for pain, vitamin D 2000 IU, and an over-the-counter glucosamine supplement; she takes no estrogen products, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or chronic steroids. She never smoked, consumes wine socially once a month, and denies illicit drug use. Review of systems is otherwise negative for chest pain, palpitations, syncope, headaches, visual changes, abdominal pain, diarrhea, melena, or neurologic deficit. On examination she rests comfortably, conversing in full sentences without distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min regular, respiratory rate 14/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body mass index is 29 kg/m². Conjunctivae are pink, sclerae clear, mucous membranes moist. Neck veins are not distended, carotid pulses are brisk, and the precordial examination reveals a nondisplaced point of maximal impulse with crisp S₁ and S₂ and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with symmetric chest expansion. Abdomen is flat with healed port-site scars in the periumbilical and suprapubic regions; bowel sounds are present, and there is no guarding or rebound. The right knee is valgus aligned, moderately enlarged, and tender along the medial joint line with crepitus on passive flexion beyond 90°, but no effusion or erythema. The left lower leg is enclosed in the intact fiberglass cast described above; capillary refill at exposed toes is brisk, pedal pulses palpate 2+, and the skin around the cast edge is intact. Both distal calves measure 35 cm in circumference with no asymmetry. Ropy subcutaneous veins course along the posterior calf bilaterally without inflammation or induration. Neurologic screening demonstrates alert mentation, intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength in the right lower limb proximally and distally, intact sensation to light touch and pinprick, and physiologic deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies drawn at 5 a.m. show hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, platelet count 246 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.84 mg/dL, AST 21 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded on admission demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 74 bpm with no ST-T abnormalities, and a portable chest radiograph is clear. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, full cervical extension, adequate inter-incisor distance, and no dental instability. She is nil per os since midnight, voided recently without difficulty, sequential compression sleeves are positioned at the bedside awaiting application in the operating theatre, and no antithrombotic medication has been administered yet pending completion of intraoperative risk assessment.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums weighted perioperative VTE risk factors.
- Age 49 (41–60 years): 1 point.
- BMI 29 kg/m² (>25): 1 point.
- Visible bilateral varicose veins: 1 point.
- Prior major surgery within one month (hysterectomy 22 days ago): 1 point.
- Current bed rest with only brief assisted transfers: 1 point. Activity at home was markedly limited, but continuous bed confinement for more than 72 hours is not established.
- Immobilizing lower-leg cast applied two weeks ago: 2 points. There was no fracture.
- Planned elective total knee replacement: 5 points. Do not also score the same operation as generic surgery lasting over 45 minutes.
Total: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 5 = 12.
Final answer: 12
